module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$

This sequence is the expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$ in powers of $x$.
It satisfies the linear recurrence relation $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$.

*References:*
- [A087455](https://oeis.org/A087455)-/

@[expose] public section

namespace OeisA87455

/-- The primary defining sequence `a`, satisfying $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$. -/
def a : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => 2 * a (n + 1) - 3 * a n

/-- The decimal significand of an integer `x`: the unique real number $S(x) \in [1, 10)$ such that
$|x| = S(x) \cdot 10^k$ for some integer $k$, with the convention $S(0) = 0$. -/
noncomputable def significand (x : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (x.natAbs : ℝ) / 10 ^ ((Nat.digits 10 x.natAbs).length - 1)

/-- A sequence of integers satisfies Benford's law if, for every $t \in [1, 10)$, the asymptotic
relative frequency of terms whose decimal significand is at most $t$ equals $\log_{10} t$
(Berger-Hill). This is strictly stronger than the law for the leading digit alone. -/
def SatisfiesBenford (s : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ t ∈ Set.Ico (1 : ℝ) 10,
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun N : ℕ =>
        ((Finset.range N).filter (fun n => significand (s n) ≤ t)).card / (N : ℝ))
      Filter.atTop
      (nhds (Real.logb 10 t))

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 0. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 1. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 2. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = -1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 3. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = -5 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 4. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = -7 := by rfl

/--
It is an open question whether or not this sequence satisfies Benford's law
[Berger-Hill, 2017; Arno Berger, email, Jan 06 2017]. - N. J. A. Sloane, Feb 08 2017-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 60]
theorem conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ SatisfiesBenford a := by
  sorry

end OeisA87455

reformulations.difference: The OEIS comment cites Berger–Hill (Notices 2017). That article poses the open question for solutions of x_n + 2x_{n-1} + 3x_{n-2} = 0 (roots -1 ± i√2). The Lean follows the OEIS and asks it for A087455, which satisfies a(n) = 2a(n-1) - 3a(n-2) (roots 1 ± i√2). A reader comparing with the Notices might think the wrong recurrence was formalized.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: b(n) := (-1)^n * a(n) satisfies b(n+2) + 2b(n+1) + 3b(n) = 0, and |b(n)| = |a(n)|. `significand` depends only on natAbs, so significand (b n) = significand (a n) for every n, hence SatisfiesBenford a ↔ SatisfiesBenford b. I proved all three in Lean (`b_rec`, `significand_neg_one_pow_mul`, `benford_twist`). So A087455 is, up to sign, a solution of the Notices recurrence and its Benford property is the same. The Lean states the OEIS question ('this sequence') literally.

reformulations.difference: The significand is computed as |x| / 10^((Nat.digits 10 |x|).length - 1), using truncated ℕ subtraction. Berger–Hill (Def. 2.3) define S(x) as the unique t ∈ [1,10) with |x| = 10^k t for some k ∈ ℤ, with S(0) := 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Proved in Lean. For x ≠ 0: 1 ≤ significand x < 10 and |x| = significand x * 10^(Nat.log 10 |x|) (`significand_spec`, via Nat.length_digits and Nat.pow_log_le_self / Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self). Any s ∈ [1,10) with |x| = s·10^k (k : ℤ) equals significand x (`significand_unique`). At x = 0, Nat.digits 10 0 = [] gives 0 - 1 = 0 in ℕ, so significand 0 = 0/1 = 0, which matches the convention S(0) = 0. Consequently SatisfiesBenford is literally Berger–Hill's Definition 3.1, with #{n < N} over the 0-indexed OEIS sequence in place of #{1 ≤ n ≤ N}; this shift is immaterial.

sources_consulted: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A087/A087455.seq (OEIS's own data repository; A087455 revision #138, Jun 28 2026 — full entry text incl. the Sloane Benford comment)

A. Berger, T. P. Hill, 'What is Benford's Law?', Notices AMS 64:2 (2017) 132-134, via http://web.archive.org/web/20250512054540/https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201702/rnoti-p132.pdf (definition of Benford sequence; 'the question of whether any solution (x_n) of the linear difference equation x_n + 2x_{n-1} + 3x_{n-2} = 0 is Benford hinges on Schanuel's conjecture')

A. Berger, T. P. Hill, 'A basic theory of Benford's Law', Probability Surveys 8 (2011) 1-126, via https://web.archive.org/web/20260717024740/https://projecteuclid.org/journals/probability-surveys/volume-8/issue-none/A-basic-theory-of-Benfords-Law/10.1214/11-PS175.pdf (Definition 2.3 significand, Definition 3.1 Benford sequence, Theorem 4.2, Definition 5.28, Theorems 5.32 and 5.37, Examples 5.27-5.38)
review.notes:
No misformalization found. Checks I ran in /workspace/review:

(1) `a`: #eval of the first 38 terms (via a fast iterative version proven equal to `a`) matches the OEIS %S/%T/%U data exactly. Tests a_0..a_4 match.

(2) `significand`: characterised and proven unique in Lean (see reformulations). Spot checks also compile: significand 2017 = 2.017, significand (-2017) = 2.017, significand 10 = 1, significand 99 = 9.9, significand (-5) = 5, significand 0 = 0.

(3) `SatisfiesBenford`: matches Berger–Hill Definition 3.1 and the Notices wording, for all t ∈ [1,10), with ≤ t, log base 10 and natural density. The division at N = 0 and the 0-based index are irrelevant to the limit. The strong (significand) form is the one the cited Berger–Hill works use; the docstring notes it is stronger than the first-digit law.

(4) `conjecture`: elaborates to `True ↔ SatisfiesBenford a` under the default answer mode. It is a neutral yes/no question matching 'whether or not this sequence satisfies Benford's law'. It is not a negated conjecture.

Status: 'research open' is consistent with the sources. The OEIS entry (rev. #138, Jun 28 2026) still calls the question open. Berger–Hill 2017 say the question 'hinges on Schanuel's conjecture'. By their Theorems 5.32/5.37, Benfordness here amounts to ℚ-independence of 1, log₁₀√3 and arctan(√2)/(2π), an open transcendence problem. A float sanity check of leading-digit frequencies for n < 200 000 matches Benford closely, so the statement is not trivially refutable.

Access limitations: oeis.org and ams.org are behind Cloudflare, so I read the OEIS entry from the official oeis/oeisdata mirror and the Notices/survey PDFs from the Wayback Machine. The arXiv API returned HTTP 429 twice; I did not retry. I could not access the Berger–Hill 2015 book, but the 2011 survey and 2017 Notices give the definitions and the status.
